Full Legal Recognition and Equal Protection for Modern Satanic Groups: A Case for Religious Equality

Introduction

In the United States and many other liberal democracies, the principle that “all men are created equal” is inscribed in the foundational documents that guarantee freedom of religion. Yet, despite this lofty ideal, a conspicuous gap persists: the law often treats some faiths as “legitimate” while dismissing others as fringe or even subversive. Modern Satanic groups—most notably The Satanic Temple (TST)—are emblematic of this disparity. Although TST meets every secular criterion used by courts to define a religion, it is frequently denied the same legal protections afforded to Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Buddhism, and other mainstream faiths. This essay argues that granting full legal recognition and equal protection under the law to modern Satanic groups is not merely a matter of fairness, but a necessary affirmation of constitutional values, secular pluralism, and the very essence of religious freedom.

1. Defining Religion in the Legal Sense

1.1 The Supreme Court’s Test

The U.S. Supreme Court has never provided a single, exhaustive definition of “religion.” Instead, it has employed a functional test, most famously articulated in United States v. Seeger (1965) and Welsh v. United States (1970). These decisions held that the term “religion” encompasses:

  1. A belief system that addresses ultimate questions of existence, purpose, and morality.
  2. A community of believers who share that system and engage in collective practices.
  3. A recognizable ritual or ceremonial life that expresses the belief system.
  4. An organization or structure that provides guidance and continuity.

These criteria are purely functional—focusing on the role a belief system plays in an individual's life rather than its doctrinal content.

1.2 Application to The Satanic Temple

  • Belief System: TST’s tenets emphasize reason, compassion, empathy, bodily autonomy, and the pursuit of knowledge. Its members affirm a belief in the “Satanic” symbol as a representation of rebellion against authoritarianism, an affirmation of the self, and a commitment to social justice. These positions constitute a comprehensive worldview that answers existential and moral questions.
  • Community: TST has chartered chapters in multiple states and countries, with thousands of members who participate in organized events, educational programs, and public advocacy. The community is cohesive, with regular meetings, online forums, and ritual observances (e.g., the “Satanic Mass,” the “Black Mass,” and “Rainbow Mass”).
  • Ritual and Ceremonial Life: TST conducts ceremonies for births, marriages, and funerals, as well as seasonal celebrations that reflect its theological stance. Its rituals are intentionally symbolic, employing Satanic iconography to convey moral and philosophical messages.
  • Organizational Structure: TST is incorporated as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, with a board of directors, bylaws, and a clear hierarchy. It hires staff, raises funds, and engages in public outreach—hallmarks of a formal religious organization.

Thus, TST satisfies the functional criteria used by the courts. Denying it the status of a religion on the basis of its name or symbolic imagery is, in effect, a content‑based discrimination that violates the First Amendment’s guarantee of religious neutrality.

2. The Constitutional Imperative: Equal Protection and Non‑Establishment

2.1 The Free Exercise Clause

The First Amendment guarantees “the free exercise” of religion. This protection is not limited to beliefs that a majority finds palatable; it explicitly shields minority faiths from governmental interference. In Employment Division v. Smith (1990), the Court held that neutral laws of general applicability do not violate the Free Exercise Clause, but subsequent decisions (e.g., Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. City of Hialeah, 1993) have reaffirmed that the government may not target a specific religious practice with discriminatory intent.

Granting legal recognition to TST would vindicate the principle that the government cannot preference one faith over another. When states extend religious exemptions (e.g., religious accommodations for conscientious objectors, tax exemptions for charitable organizations, or the right to meet for worship), the denial of those same benefits to a Satanic group amounts to unconstitutional discrimination.

2.2 The Establishment Clause

Ironically, the very clause intended to prevent government endorsement of religion can be invoked to justify exclusion of minority faiths. However, the Supreme Court’s jurisprudence consistently warns against “endorsement” of any religion, not just the majority’s. In County of Allegheny v. ACLU (1989), the Court emphasized that the government must be a “neutral observer,” not a partisan adjudicator of which religions are worthy of recognition. By denying TST the same legal standing, the state effectively endorses a particular conception of “acceptable” religion, thereby violating the neutrality required by the Establishment Clause.

2.3 Equal Protection Under the Law

The Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause forbids the state from denying any person the equal protection of the laws. When the government bestows benefits (tax exemptions, charitable status, educational accreditation, or the right to display religious symbols on public property) exclusively on majority religions, it creates a “class” of favored religions and a “class” of disfavored ones. This classification must be subject to “strict scrutiny” because it implicates a fundamental right—freedom of religion. Under strict scrutiny, the government must demonstrate a compelling interest and must employ the least restrictive means. There is no compelling interest that justifies excluding TST, especially when its beliefs and practices satisfy the same legal tests applied to other faiths.

3. The Social Value of Satanic Philosophy

3.1 Emphasis on Reason and Individual Autonomy

TST’s core tenets champion rational inquiry, scientific literacy, and personal responsibility. In an era where misinformation and polarization threaten democratic institutions, a religious movement that prizes reason and critical thinking offers a constructive counter‑narrative. Recognizing TST legally would signal that the state values intellectual rigor and the empowerment of individuals to think for themselves.

3.2 Commitment to Social Justice

3.3 Fostering Pluralism

A pluralistic society thrives when diverse worldviews coexist under the law. Recognizing TST expands the religious landscape, encouraging dialogue and mutual respect among faith traditions. It also serves as a safeguard: when the state can silence a minority faith today, the precedent may be used to marginalize other minority religions tomorrow. 4.1 “Satanism is Offensive”

The offensiveness of a religion’s symbols is not a constitutionally permissible basis for denial of rights.
